title: Let us live and love
author: Catullus

edition.name: Catullus, edited by Elmer Truesdell Merrill (Boston: Ginn and Company, 1893), public domain; the Perseus Digital Library TEI text (PerseusDL canonical-latinLit, phi0472.phi001.perseus-lat2), whose header credits "Elmer Truesdell Merrill", "Ginn and Company", "1893"

source_text:
Vivamus, mea Lesbia, atque amemus,
rumoresque senum severiorum
omnes unius aestimemus assis.
soles occidere et redire possunt:
nobis, cum semel occidit brevis lux,
nox est perpetua una dormienda.
excerpt_note: The first six of the poem's thirteen lines, as printed; the poem goes on to the kisses (line 7, da mi basia mille).

macrons.note: Macrons are editorial: added by Vocābula, not printed in the edition. Vowel quantities follow the app lexicon (Wheelock / DCC spellings) where the word is in it, and standard dictionary quantities otherwise.
uncertain: ūnīus: the app spells the genitive with long ī, the normal prose quantity; in this line Catullus scans it short (ūnĭus), as the meter requires.
occidere, occidit: short i (occidō, "fall, set", from ob + cadō), not occīdō, "kill" (ob + caedō); not machine-checked.
sevēriōrum: long ē in the second syllable, as in sevērus; not machine-checked.
rūmōrēs: long ū and ō, as in rūmor, rūmōris; not machine-checked.
amēmus, aestimēmus, atque: in recitation final syllables elide before vowels (mea Lesbia atque amemus); the macrons show each word's own quantities.

tokens.parse: gen. sg. (genitive of value, with assis)

tokens.gloss: as (a small coin): at one penny
to set, to go down (not occīdō, "kill")

tokens.parse: dat. pl. (dative of agent with dormienda)
gerundive, nom. sg. f. (with est: passive periphrastic, "must be slept")

translation: Let us live, my Lesbia, and let us love, and let us value all the gossip of over-strict old men at a single penny. Suns can set and come back again; but we, once our brief light has set, must sleep through one never-ending night.
translation_note: The as was a small coin; "a single penny" gives the idea of ūnīus assis, a genitive of value. nōbīs is a dative of agent with the gerundive dormienda: literally "one everlasting night must be slept by us". The two senses of occidere, the sun setting and a life ending, are the point of lines 4-6.

essay.t: Poem 5 begins as an invitation: let us live and love, and value the gossip of censorious old men at a single as, that is, at next to nothing.
Merrill's edition labels its meter Phalaecean, the eleven-syllable line it assigns to about forty of the poems; that count is mine, from the edition's meter labels.
Lines 4 to 6 give the reason for hurry: suns can set and return, but for us, once our brief light has set, there is one everlasting night to be slept.
The contrast is between many suns that come back and a single night that does not, and the same verb, occidere, serves for a sunset and for a death; this is my reading, not a sourced claim.
If the accepted dates of about 84 to 54 BC are right, Catullus himself died at about thirty.
The poem then turns to arithmetic: give me a thousand kisses, then a hundred, then another thousand, until the lovers muddle the count so that they themselves will not know it.

The last line gives a second reason: so that no ill-wisher can invidere, cast the evil eye, by knowing how many kisses there were; reading invidere as the evil eye is a common interpretation, and mine here, rather than something the text states.
Lesbia is generally taken as a pseudonym.
Apuleius, in the second century AD, says that Catullus used the name Lesbia for Clodia.
Britannica treats that identification with caution, noting that it also rests on uncertain inferences from the poems themselves and that it is not certain which Clodia is meant.
What is not in doubt is the poem itself, whose opening line is one of the most quoted in Latin; that it is much quoted is my own judgment rather than a measured fact.

questions.q: What are the old men's rumors worth, according to the speaker?
options: A single small coin, next to nothing
Charges to report to the magistrates
Verses worth answering in a poem
Suns set and return; our light, once set, does not
Day is for work, while night is for love
The young are wise, while the old are foolish
Rome is great, while Verona is small

questions.q: Why should the lovers confuse the count of their kisses?
options: So no ill-wisher can cast the evil eye by knowing it
Because Catullus could not count that high
So that they could win a bet with their friends
Because the meter needed extra syllables
